analysis.one_liner: Cuts greenhouse gas emissions every year and requires 20% renewable electricity by 2020.
analysis.headline: The Safe Climate Act drew 155 House cosponsors — 153 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required U.S. greenhouse gas emissions to fall about 2% per year starting in 2010, returning to 1990 levels by 2020 and dropping to 20% of 1990 levels by 2050. It set up a cap-and-trade system with penalties for excess emissions, required car emissions standards at least as strict as California's, required 20% of retail electricity to come from renewable sources by 2020, and directed money from allowance auctions into a fund to help consumers and workers with energy cost increases. It never got a vote in committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit from steady cuts in the pollution driving climate change — the bill's own findings cite heat waves, wildfires, sea level rise, and drought already underway. Low-income households would get help paying higher energy bills from the Climate Reinvestment Fund, and workers and regions dependent on coal and other high-carbon energy would receive transition assistance. The renewable electricity and efficiency mandates would also push down energy waste and, over time, consumer costs, while the savings clause preserved states' rights to act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, low-income households, and future generations

how_it_helps.text: Sets annual greenhouse gas reduction targets: emissions freeze at 2009 levels in 2010, fall about 2% per year to reach 1990 levels by 2020, then fall about 5% per year so that 2050 emissions are no more than 20% of 1990 levels.
Requires vehicle emissions standards at least as strict as California's September 2004 standards, revised every five years to go further.
Requires that at least 20% of retail electricity come from renewable sources by 2020, and sets annual energy-savings targets for electric and gas suppliers to cut their customers' usage.

Creates a Climate Reinvestment Fund from allowance auction proceeds and penalties, dedicated to easing energy cost increases for consumers (especially low-income households) and providing transition assistance to workers and regions moving away from high-carbon energy.

Enforces the cap with real penalties: companies that exceed their emissions must surrender allowances and pay a civil penalty of twice the market price of an allowance per unit of excess emissions, and requires emissions to be accurately tracked, reported, and verified.
Includes a savings clause ensuring the bill does not preempt or limit state climate actions.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning utilities, oil companies, and other large emitters would bear the cost of buying allowances, cutting emissions, and paying penalties of twice the allowance price for excess pollution. Households could face some near-term energy price increases, though the bill directed auction proceeds toward cushioning those increases, particularly for low-income consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal utilities and other large emitters

drawbacks.text: A nationwide emissions cap and renewable mandate would likely raise electricity and fuel prices in the short run; the bill itself acknowledges this by directing auction proceeds toward 'mitigating the effect of any energy cost increases to consumers, particularly low-income consumers.'

The cap-and-trade design creates a new market in emission allowances whose prices would fluctuate, and gives the President discretion over how allowances are distributed — a structure that requires careful enforcement to avoid favoritism, though the bill explicitly bars free allocations that create windfall profits for covered entities.

The bill included its own escape valve: the EPA Administrator could extend the first emissions deadlines of 2009-2011 by one or two years if that would substantially reduce compliance costs, which supporters of faster action might see as delaying the early cuts scientists said were necessary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest objection is real: an economy-wide carbon cap and a 20% renewable mandate would raise energy prices for households and squeeze energy-intensive industries, which is why the bill built a fund specifically to offset cost increases for low-income consumers and to assist displaced energy workers. Against that is the bill's core finding that emissions must start falling within a decade to keep warming below the 2°C threshold scientists identified, and that clean-energy and efficiency measures could save consumers money over time. The bill was honestly designed — it barred windfall profits, created enforcement penalties, and left state protections intact — but it was never debated, so its costs and design were never tested in public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's energy subcommittee from March 2007 until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009, never getting a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Safe Climate Act of 2007 in the House on March 20, 2007, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs Committees the same day.
It quickly drew 155 cosponsors, 153 of them Democrats and 2 Republicans.
On March 21, 2007, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning utilities and other large emitters were better off because the bill never advanced, since they avoided a nationwide emissions cap and the renewable electricity mandate. Ordinary people got none of the emissions reductions or clean-energy requirements the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Climate Act of 2007 and promoted it with introductory remarks on March 21, 2007.

for.name: Reps. Frank LoBiondo and Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Were the bill's only two Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled it for a markup or committee vote during the 110th Congress.

against.name: Coal and electric utility interests
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandatory economy-wide emissions caps and renewable electricity mandates during the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 153 of the 155 cosponsors were House Democrats, with just 2 Republicans — and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The emissions cap, penalty structure, and requirement that 20% of retail electricity be renewable by 2020 would directly force utilities burning coal to cut output or buy allowances. Avoiding this obligation was the main material benefit of the bill never advancing.

A steadily tightening cap on the largest emitters, combined with a national renewable electricity standard, would shrink the market for coal over time. The bill's failure preserved coal's share of power generation for another decade.

Vehicle greenhouse gas standards matching California's 2004 rules, tightened every five years, would push fuel efficiency and alternative vehicles at the expense of gasoline demand. The bill's death left federal fuel-emission policy unchanged at the time.

The 20% renewable electricity standard and cumulative end-user efficiency targets would have guaranteed a growing market for wind, solar, and efficiency services. The bill's failure removed that guaranteed demand.
The bill authorized trading of emission allowances by any person, creating a new financial market. The gains are uncertain and contingent — they existed only if the cap was enacted.
